data.text/markdown:
What New York's street-level flood sensors can tell us

FloodNet is a network of cheap ultrasonic sensors, run by NYU and CUNY with city agencies, that measures water depth on New York streets every minute. NYC Open Data publishes every flood event the sensors have recorded since 2020. This notebook does the analysis a city would want from that feed and checks four things:
  1. The network today: sensors and events in the feed, against the 87 sensors and 360 events (October 2020 to May 2023) in the FloodNet team's 2024 paper.
  2. Rain or tide: each event checked against NOAA tide gauges and airport rain gauges.
  3. Mapped risk: how many flooding sensors and events sit outside FEMA's flood zones and outside the city's Stormwater Flood Maps.
  4. What's nearby: schools, hospitals, fire and EMS stations, nursing homes and subway entrances near the sensors that flood most often.
It ends with the Hurricane Ida "50 minutes early" claim and what didn't work. What it can't show: flooding where there is no sensor. FloodNet puts sensors at places already known to flood, so these are not a random sample of the city. Issue #213. Data: FloodNet (New York University and The City University of New York), Mydlarz et al. (2024).

1. The network today

Two NYC Open Data tables, downloaded fresh on every run: sensor deployment metadata (kb2e-tjy3) and flood events (aq7i-eu5q). FloodNet defines an event as a run of readings deeper than 10 mm that its team has checked by hand. Many events are shallow, so we also count floods: events whose peak reached 4 inches at the sensor, the bottom of the "nuisance" tier in the city's Stormwater Flood Maps (a rule we take from Mark Bauer's FloodNet tutorials).

data.text/markdown: As of the data cutoff (2026-11-09), the feed lists 496 sensors ever deployed, 452 still active, and 3,611 events at 322 sensors, of which 1,602 reached 4 inches. The 2024 paper's two numbers come from different dates: 87 sensors installed "as of February 2024", and 360 events its team classed as floods out of 6,641 raw events from October 2020 to May 2023. Today's feed lists 97 sensors installed before March 2024, so the network is now about 5.7 times the paper's size by sensors ever deployed. For October 2020 to May 2023 the feed has 278 events at 19 sensors, not 360. The feed doesn't say why; FloodNet's events go through manual review, and the paper's count may include events the published feed leaves out or splits differently. Sensors are not spread evenly: compare the boroughs above. A few coastal sensors that flood with the tide account for many of the events, which is why the next step splits them out.

2. Rain or tide?

FloodNet marks each sensor as tidally influenced or not, and Bauer's tutorials split the record on that flag. But the flag is per sensor, not per event: a coastal sensor can flood in a downpour at low tide. So we check each event against what the water and the sky were doing at the time.
  • When the water peaked. Each event carries its minute-by-minute depth profile; the peak time is the start time plus the offset of the deepest reading.
  • Tide. NOAA CO-OPS 6-minute water levels at the nearest of three tide gauges with a full record since 2020: the Battery, Kings Point and Sandy Hook, measured against each gauge's own Mean High Water (MHW). The tide counts if the water at the gauge was at or above MHW within 90 minutes of the peak.
  • Rain. Hourly rain at the nearest of four airport weather stations (Central Park, LaGuardia, JFK and Newark), from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet's free ASOS archive. Rain counts if at least 0.10 inch fell from 3 hours before the event started to the peak.
That gives four classes: rain only, tide only, both, and neither. The rules are ours. Bauer's tutorials use only the sensor flag and flood timing, so the per-event method here is new; the thresholds are judgment calls, and a sensitivity table below shows how much they matter.

data.text/markdown: Why the tide only counts where FloodNet says it reaches. Water at a gauge is within 90 minutes of being above MHW about 37% of the time, twice a day, every day. At sensors FloodNet flags as non-tidal, 53% of events happen near a high tide, so a gauge-only rule would label many inland downpours as tidal. The rule above therefore lets the tide explain an event only at sensors FloodNet flags as tidally influenced, and uses the gauges and rain to sort the events at those sensors. The flag still can't catch a high tide backing up an outfall and flooding an inland street. "Neither" means the nearest airport gauge saw under 0.10 inch and the tide didn't qualify: a downpour that missed the airport gauges, a sensor glitch, snow, or a tide that runs higher or later in a bay than at the gauge (Jamaica Bay has no long-running NOAA gauge). How much do the thresholds matter? The same shares (% of all events) under looser and stricter rules, with rain taken at whichever of the four stations saw the most, and with the gauges alone deciding the tide:

data.text/markdown:
3. Inside or outside the mapped risk?

Two kinds of map, made for different floods:
  • FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer maps coastal and river flooding: the 1% annual chance floodplain (the Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA) and the 0.2% zone. It does not map flooding from rain overwhelming the sewers. We ask FEMA's live NFHL service which zone each sensor sits in (the same identify call our critical-facilities-flood-zones/ spike uses).
  • NYC's Stormwater Flood Maps model rain flooding of at least 4 inches over at least a quarter acre. We use two of the four published scenarios: Moderate (2.13 in/hr, current sea levels) and the widest, Extreme (3.66 in/hr with 2080 sea level rise, which adds a "future high tides" layer).
Sensors hang over sidewalks, while the modeled ponding is mostly in the roadway, so we count a sensor as inside a stormwater area if it is within 20 m of one, and report the strict point-in-polygon count too.

data.text/markdown:
Of the 199 sensors that have recorded at least one 4-inch flood, 60.8% sit outside FEMA's 1% floodplain and 36.2% are more than 20 m from the city's moderate stormwater flood areas. Each map misses the other kind of flood:
  • Rain-only floods: 67.3% happened outside the SFHA, as you'd expect, since FEMA doesn't map rain flooding. The stormwater map does better: 29.9% were more than 20 m from its moderate scenario, and 20.1% from the rain layers of its most extreme scenario.
  • Tide-only floods: 0.2% outside the SFHA, but 93.1% outside the moderate stormwater map, which models rain only.
  • Together, FEMA's 0.2% zone plus the extreme 2080 stormwater scenario (whose "future high tides" layer covers most of the shoreline) leave 0.0% of flooding sensors unmapped.
So the sensors don't find flooding the maps have never imagined. They show which map applies where, and that someone reading only the FEMA map would miss most of the places the sensors record rain flooding. Remember the selection, too: FloodNet puts sensors where flooding is known or expected (see Bauer's notes on the FloodNet data description and Ceferino et al. 2023), so none of this estimates what the maps miss citywide.

4. What's near the sensors that flood most often?

Frequently flooding here means a sensor deployed at least 180 days (Bauer's minimum, so one early flood can't make a rate) that averaged at least 4 floods of 4 inches or more a year while deployed. Deployment time assumes the sensor was always online, so rates are a lower bound. Nearby means within 250 m, about one long Manhattan block. Facilities come from HIFLD Next (public schools, open hospitals, fire and EMS stations, nursing homes), and subway entrances from the MTA's 2024 list on data.ny.gov. All are clipped to the five boroughs.

data.text/markdown:
5. The Hurricane Ida "50 minutes early" claim

Partly verified, with a narrower meaning. The FloodNet team's own paper (Mydlarz et al. 2024, section 4.3) says: "During Hurricane Ida (1 Sept 2021), the FloodNet system alerted NYC Emergency Management of flooding recorded by the sensors installed in the Gowanus neighborhood in Brooklyn 50 min before they received other notifications of the event." So the 50 minutes is lead time over other reports reaching NYC Emergency Management, not a forecast, and it is the authors' statement: we found no NYC Emergency Management document that confirms it. NYU's October 2021 press release was more cautious ("early indications that these warnings were received prior to warnings from other city detection systems"). Safe wording: according to the FloodNet team, its alerts reached NYC Emergency Management 50 minutes before other notifications of the Gowanus flooding. What the published feed shows for the Ida evening, in New York time:

data.text/markdown:
What didn't work, and what this doesn't show

  • No sensor, no record. The analysis covers only places with a sensor, and FloodNet chose those places because they were known to flood.
  • The per-event cause is approximate. Airport rain gauges miss summer cells that soak one neighbourhood, and the three NOAA gauges miss the tidal lag and amplification inside Jamaica Bay, where many tidal sensors are. "Neither" collects those misses.
  • One stormwater scenario would not open. The Limited Flood geodatabase in the city's download uses a compressed format GDAL's open driver can't read, so we used Moderate and Extreme 2080.
  • FEMA's effective NFHL for New York City is the 2007 map. FEMA's 2015 preliminary maps are larger but not in the NFHL service.
  • Deployment time assumes the sensor was always online. The feed has no uptime record.
